::: {.kw-overview}
Cardiovascular assessment of the transplant candidate dominates this issue, and two of the papers are guidance documents rather than primary studies. A joint British Transplantation Society and British Cardiovascular Society statement sets out UK recommendations on invasive coronary angiography and elective revascularisation before listing, while a European Renal Best Practice document from the ERA DESCaRTES group and ESOT's EKITA committee tackles the adjacent and equally awkward problem of antithrombotic drugs in candidates and recipients — including how long to stop aspirin before an allograft biopsy. Two cohorts sharpen the same pre-listing assessment from different angles: one shows that pre-transplant heart failure with preserved ejection fraction behaves as a persistent, non-reversible phenotype after transplantation whereas reduced ejection fraction largely recovers, and another finds that two widely used frailty instruments identify genuinely different at-risk patients rather than the same ones. On immunosuppression and infection, a meta-analysis finds no overall excess cancer risk with belatacept compared with calcineurin inhibitors but flags conversion as the subgroup to watch, and a phase 3 subgroup analysis shows letermovir markedly outperforming valganciclovir on adherence and myelotoxicity in recipients aged 65 and over. The issue closes on access and equity, with the first nationwide UK description of what happens after a transplant fails — showing clear ethnic, socioeconomic and sex-related inequalities in pre-emptive re-transplantation — alongside five-year psychosocial follow-up of living kidney donors that should reassure donor assessment clinics.
:::

---

### 1. [Joint British Transplantation Society and British Cardiovascular Society guideline on invasive coronary angiography and elective coronary artery revascularisation in adult potential kidney transplant recipients](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trre.2026.101049)
[Ludman A, Corr M, Ferro C, Fossati N, Graham-Brown M, Howse M, Jeetley P, Jones G, Kelly D, Kojro A, Lioudaki E, McGill L, Madden B, Nagaraja P, Nimmo A, Sharif A, Wijetunga I, Asgari E. *Transplant Rev (Orlando)*, 2026. PMID: 42641294.]{.kw-ref}

Cardiac work-up before transplant listing has long varied between UK centres, and this paper is the joint British Transplantation Society and British Cardiovascular Society response to that variation. The authors note that cardiovascular disease remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in both kidney transplant candidates and recipients, which is the stated rationale for investigating the heart before listing at all — the aim being to minimise early post-operative cardiac events and premature death. The parent guideline, on cardiovascular assessment of potential adult kidney transplant recipients, was written explicitly to harmonise UK practice, and this manuscript extracts and summarises the recommendations from the chapters dealing with invasive coronary angiography and coronary revascularisation. The central message the authors draw out is one of evidential restraint: invasive coronary angiography and revascularisation may be considered as part of the pre-transplant work-up, but there is limited evidence supporting that strategy in asymptomatic patients. The author list spans transplant nephrology, transplant surgery and cardiology across Exeter, Belfast, Birmingham, London, Leicester, Liverpool, Derby, Sheffield, Cardiff, Bristol and Manchester, which is itself an indication of how much the recommendations are intended to be a national standard rather than local opinion. The abstract summarises scope and intent rather than reproducing the graded recommendations or any supporting effect estimates, so the specific thresholds and strength of each recommendation have to be read in the full guideline. For a UK unit, this is the document that should now anchor local pre-listing cardiac protocols, and its scepticism about routine invasive investigation of asymptomatic candidates is the part most likely to change what a listing meeting actually asks for.

### 2. [Management of antithrombotic therapies in kidney transplantation candidates and recipients: an ERBP clinical practice document by the DESCaRTES Working Group of ERA and the EKITA Committee of ESOT](https://doi.org/10.1093/ndt/gfag024)
[Velioglu A, Karagiannidis AG, Demir E, Hellemans R, Gandolfini I, Thomas R, de Weerd A, Dedinska I, Kousios A, Samoš M, Küçükkaya RD, Erlandsson H, Sharif A, Schiffer M, Mariat C, Hilbrands L. *Nephrol Dial Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 41661128.]{.kw-ref}

Patients with end-stage kidney disease sit on both sides of the haemostatic balance at once, and the major anticoagulation trials excluded them, leaving transplant clinicians to extrapolate — the gap this European Renal Best Practice document sets out to fill. The panel, drawn from the ERA DESCaRTES working group and ESOT's EKITA committee with added cardiology, haematology and methodology input, framed four clinical questions and answered them through a systematic review conducted to PRISMA and ERBP principles. The scale of the problem is set out in the background: the authors cite rates of newly diagnosed cerebrovascular events and myocardial infarction of up to 6.8% and 11.1% respectively within three years of transplantation, almost 9% of recipients developing venous thromboembolism within five years — a sevenfold excess over the general population — severe post-transplant bleeding at around 4%, and graft thrombosis in under 1% of transplants. On peri-operative risk the evidence they found was uniformly weak, heterogeneous and at high risk of bias, though a pooled analysis they cite showed dual antiplatelet therapy raised post-operative haemorrhage risk by almost 60% compared with monotherapy, and two separate cohorts found continued vitamin K antagonist use independently associated with roughly six-fold higher odds of post-operative bleeding. The resulting practice points are pragmatic rather than prescriptive: individualise the decision to continue, interrupt or modify therapy according to expected waiting time, availability of reversal agents and centre experience; avoid direct oral anticoagulants in waitlisted patients given how thin the transplant-surgery safety data are; and accept that heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin thromboprophylaxis after transplantation is not associated with increased bleeding. For recipients the panel declines to favour DOACs over vitamin K antagonists on current evidence, urges close monitoring of graft function because of dose-dependence, counsels caution below a GFR of 30 mL/min/1.73 m², and notes that DOAC–calcineurin inhibitor interactions mostly appear clinically insignificant — though ticagrelor is singled out elsewhere as needing caution with ciclosporin. The most immediately usable output is on biopsy: low-dose aspirin at 150 mg/day or less generally does not raise bleeding risk if stopped at least three to seven days beforehand, continuation within three days of biopsy may increase bleeding, higher doses above 300 mg warrant five to seven days, and clopidogrel should be considered for discontinuation at least seven days before. The authors are candid that no bleeding or thrombosis risk score — HAS-BLED and CHA₂DS₂-VASc included — has been validated in this population, so UK units should treat this as a structured framework for individualised decisions rather than a rulebook.

### 3. [Distinct Prognostic Trajectories of Heart Failure Phenotypes Following Kidney Transplantation](https://doi.org/10.1093/eschf/xvag221)
[Bril M, Imam A, Parnasa E, Rivin M, Shabaneh S, Tzukert K, Roai A, Amir O, Khalaileh A, Asleh R. *ESC Heart Fail*, 2026. PMID: 42619645.]{.kw-ref}

Transplantation is often assumed to reverse uraemic cardiomyopathy, and this retrospective cohort asks whether that assumption holds equally for both heart failure phenotypes. The investigators stratified 442 adult kidney transplant recipients by pre-transplant echocardiography into heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (ejection fraction ≥50% with elevated filling pressures, 64 patients, 14.5%), heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (ejection fraction <50%, 44 patients, 10.0%), and 334 controls (75.5%), then followed longitudinal echocardiographic remodelling and clinical outcomes with multivariable Cox regression over a median 49 months. The preserved-ejection-fraction group fared markedly worse: it was independently associated with heart failure hospitalisation (adjusted HR 9.57; 95% CI 3.37–27.2; p < 0.001) and with the composite of death or heart failure hospitalisation (adjusted HR 4.46; 95% CI 2.36–8.42; p < 0.001), and paired echocardiography showed diastolic stiffness that did not resolve (E/e′ 12.7 ± 4.6 to 11.8 ± 5.3; p = 0.117). The reduced-ejection-fraction group behaved quite differently, recovering systolic function by a mean of 8.7 ± 10.2 percentage points (p = 0.003) and remaining independently associated with all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 2.9; 95% CI 1.16–7.25; p = 0.023) but not with heart failure hospitalisation (adjusted HR 3.11; 95% CI 0.71–13.6; p = 0.13). Mechanistically, the change in ejection fraction predicted lower hospitalisation risk (adjusted HR 0.94; 95% CI 0.90–0.99; p = 0.02), while mortality tracked with changes in haemoglobin (adjusted HR 0.71; 95% CI 0.60–0.83; p < 0.001) and calcium (adjusted HR 0.69; 95% CI 0.50–0.96; p = 0.027). The authors conclude that uraemic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction is a persistent, non-reversible phenotype and argue for targeted diastolic profiling at assessment rather than an ejection-fraction-centred read of the echocardiogram. Set against the BTS/BCS guidance above, this is a useful corrective for UK listing practice — the candidate whose ejection fraction looks acceptable may be the one carrying the higher post-transplant burden — though the single-centre retrospective design and small phenotype subgroups, reflected in the very wide confidence intervals, mean the effect sizes should be read as directional rather than precise.

### 4. [Performance-Based Frailty Tools Capture Distinct Risk Phenotypes in Kidney Transplant Candidates: A Comparative Analysis of FRAIL and SPPB](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2026.08.014)
[Verhoeff R, Hullekes FE, Jaffe E, Cataldo JL, Rockenbach MABC, Bizzo BC, Pratt HM, Foster P, Lee SA, Melaragno N, Warner A, Nissaisorakarn P, Elias N, Shah SA, Gilligan HM, de Bruin RWF, Porte RJ, Riella LV. *Am J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42641925.]{.kw-ref}

Frailty is now routinely measured in transplant candidates, but whether different instruments are interchangeable has not been established — the question this retrospective cohort addresses directly. The authors assessed 953 candidates listed between 2018 and 2022 with both the questionnaire-based FRAIL scale (fatigue, resistance, ambulation, illnesses, weight loss) and the performance-based Short Physical Performance Battery, and in a subset with available CT imaging analysed body composition using AI-based tools. The two instruments disagreed substantially on who was frail at all: prevalence was 6.2% by FRAIL against 24% by SPPB. Waitlist mortality occurred in 9.5% of candidates (91 of 953), and both tools independently predicted it, though FRAIL more strongly (adjusted HR 2.38, 95% CI 1.34–4.20, p = 0.003) than SPPB (adjusted HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.07–2.60, p = 0.025). The pattern reversed after transplantation, where SPPB-defined frailty showed the stronger associations — with longer hospital stay and with both 30-day and one-year readmissions — and the CT substudy gave that a plausible mechanism, since SPPB-defined but not FRAIL-defined frailty was associated with lower muscle density and greater visceral adiposity. The authors read this as evidence that the two capture complementary dimensions, FRAIL reflecting symptom burden and waitlist mortality risk, SPPB reflecting the physical substrate that predicts post-operative complications, and they argue for using both to stratify risk and to select candidates for targeted prehabilitation. For UK units running prehabilitation programmes or building frailty into listing assessment, the practical implication is that picking a single instrument on grounds of convenience will systematically miss one of these groups, though the single-centre retrospective design and the absence of external validation mean the case for routine dual assessment rests on association rather than on demonstrated outcome benefit.

### 5. [Cancer Risk in Kidney Transplant Recipients on Belatacept Versus Calcineurin Inhibitors: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1097/TP.0000000000005856)
[Hannouneh ZA, Issa M, Mizuno H, Murakami N. *Transplantation*, 2026. PMID: 42649552.]{.kw-ref}

Belatacept's favourable renal and cardiovascular profile has driven its uptake since approval in 2011, but its long-term malignancy risk — skin cancer in particular — has remained incompletely characterised, which is the gap this systematic review and meta-analysis addresses. The authors pooled 13 studies comprising 3,070 kidney transplant recipients, drawn from 10 randomised controlled trials and 3 observational cohorts, comparing belatacept-based against calcineurin-inhibitor-based maintenance regimens, and calculated pooled risk estimates for skin cancers and for cancers overall. Across all included studies there was no statistically significant difference in skin cancer risk (OR 1.01; 95% CI 0.67–1.52) or in all cancers (OR 1.14; 95% CI 0.69–1.88). The more interesting signal emerged from a prespecified subgroup comparison by how belatacept was started: patients converted from a calcineurin inhibitor showed a trend towards higher risk of both skin cancers (OR 1.82; 95% CI 0.43–7.63) and all cancers (OR 1.83; 95% CI 0.99–3.39), whereas those started on de novo belatacept did not (skin cancer OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.68–1.06; all cancers OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.41–2.09). Every one of those subgroup confidence intervals crosses unity, and the skin cancer estimate in particular is extremely imprecise, so this is a hypothesis about conversion rather than a demonstration of harm. The authors' own conclusion is appropriately restrained — no significant excess overall, with larger studies powered on cancer as a primary endpoint needed to characterise the conversion signal properly. For UK practice, where belatacept use is comparatively limited and conversion is often considered for calcineurin-inhibitor nephrotoxicity, the reassurance on overall cancer risk is useful, while the conversion subgroup is a reason to maintain the usual dermatological surveillance rather than to withhold conversion.

### 6. [Favorable Adherence and Tolerability of Letermovir Versus Valganciclovir for Cytomegalovirus Prophylaxis in Kidney Transplant Recipients Aged 65 y or Older: Findings From a Randomized, Phase 3 Trial](https://doi.org/10.1097/TXD.0000000000001990)
[Bunnapradist S, Vincenti F, Witzke O, Schneeberger S, Nguyen MH, Broyde N, Gilbert CL, Haber B. *Transplant Direct*, 2026. PMID: 42639594.]{.kw-ref}

Older recipients now make up a growing share of the transplant population and tolerate valganciclovir's myelotoxicity poorly, which makes this age-stratified analysis of a randomised trial directly relevant to prophylaxis policy. The phase 3, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled P002 study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03443869) compared 200 days of letermovir against valganciclovir prophylaxis in cytomegalovirus-seronegative kidney transplant recipients of kidneys from seropositive donors — the highest-risk D+/R− serostatus — and this report covers the 48 letermovir and 55 valganciclovir participants aged 65 or older. Committee-confirmed cytomegalovirus disease through week 52 post-transplant occurred in 9% of the letermovir group versus 22% of the valganciclovir group, a stratum-adjusted difference of −12% (95% CI −27% to 2%), which does not exclude no difference; the authors report no significant between-group differences in cytomegalovirus disease or viraemia. Where letermovir clearly separated was in deliverability and safety. Adherence of 90% or greater was achieved by 96% of letermovir recipients (95% CI 86%–100%) against 49% on valganciclovir (95% CI 35%–63%), and leukopenia or neutropenia through week 28 affected 31% (95% CI 19%–46%) versus 62% (95% CI 48%–75%) — both significant differences. Drug-related adverse events (25% versus 49%), discontinuations for adverse events (10% versus 20%), opportunistic infections (11% versus 25%) and rehospitalisations through week 52 (51% versus 69%) all favoured letermovir numerically. The authors conclude that letermovir offers substantial advantages in adherence, safety and tolerability in this age group, and for UK units the halving of cytomegalovirus-prophylaxis-attributable cytopenias in older D+/R− recipients — with the knock-on effect on mycophenolate dose reductions and rehospitalisation — is the argument most likely to carry weight in a formulary discussion, tempered by the small subgroup size and the fact that the efficacy comparison was not powered at this stratum.

### 7. [Inequalities in outcomes after kidney transplant failure in the UK](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0356769)
[Westaway S, Bailey PK, Santhakumaran S, Beresford M, Greenhall G, Griffin S, Hole BD, Hilton R, Masoud S, Nitsch D, Plumb L, Robb M, Pippias M. *PLoS One*, 2026. PMID: 42647538.]{.kw-ref}

Roughly a quarter of UK kidney transplants fail within ten years, yet what happens to those patients afterwards has never been described nationally — the gap this first output of the FAKTOR study fills. Using UK Renal Registry data from England, Wales and Northern Ireland, the authors retrospectively followed 5,447 adults whose transplant failed (defined as eGFR below 15 mL/min/1.73 m²) between January 2012 and December 2021, classifying treatment status each year and modelling one-year outcomes with multilevel multinomial regression mutually adjusted for age, sex, ethnicity, deprivation quintile, primary renal disease and centre type. By one year, 47.8% had started haemodialysis, 26.4% remained alive without new kidney replacement therapy, 10.8% had started peritoneal dialysis, 9.3% had died, and only 5.2% had been pre-emptively re-transplanted. Access to that re-transplantation was strikingly unequal: Black people were 59% less likely (RRR 0.41, 95% CI 0.20–0.87) and Asian people 43% less likely (RRR 0.57, 0.34–0.96) to be re-transplanted than White people, each quintile increase in deprivation carried a 22% lower likelihood (RRR 0.78, 0.71–0.86), and males were more likely than females both to be re-transplanted (RRR 1.39, 1.06–1.81) and to start haemodialysis (RRR 1.68, 1.47–1.92). The authors set the ethnic gap in context: Black people are already 34% less likely to receive a first transplant in the UK, so a 59% deficit at pre-emptive re-transplantation represents a widening rather than a persisting disparity, plausibly driven in part by cumulative immunological disadvantage — minority ethnic groups made up 7% of UK deceased kidney donors in 2024/25 but 35% of the active transplant list. Practice differed by centre too, with pre-dialysis eGFR 7.1% higher in non-transplanting than transplanting centres (+7.1%, 95% CI +2.6% to +11.9%), meaning dialysis started earlier away from transplant centres, alongside weak evidence of less re-transplantation there (RRR 0.66, 0.43–1.00); diabetic primary renal disease nearly doubled the risk of death relative to glomerulonephritis (RRR 1.97, 1.34–2.88). The authors are clear about what registry data cannot settle — there is no tissue typing, sensitisation, re-listing or detailed comorbidity information, and their eGFR-based definition of failure probably over-counts patients with stable but poor function — but for UK units this is direct evidence that the failing-transplant clinic is where inequity in access is being generated, and an argument for auditing local re-listing practice by ethnicity and deprivation.

### 8. [Donor Self-Esteem Before and After Living Kidney Donation](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.ajkd.2026.05.023)
[Neumann R, Arnold JB, Boudville N, Cuerden MS, Dew MA, Dipchand C, Feldman LS, Gill JS, Karpinski M, Klarenbach S, Knoll GA, Lok C, Miller M, Monroy-Caudros M, Naylor KL, Nguan C, Prasad GVR, Sontrop JM, Storsley L, Stronks K, Garg AX. *Am J Kidney Dis*, 2026. PMID: 42637175.]{.kw-ref}

Living donors are known to have normal-to-high self-esteem before donating, but whether donation itself erodes that over the following years — and which donors are vulnerable — has been poorly characterised, which this prospective cohort set out to establish. The investigators enrolled 941 living kidney donors before donation at 12 Canadian and 5 Australian transplant centres between 2009 and 2014, measuring self-esteem with the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (range 0–30, higher scores better) before donation, at 3 months, and then annually for five years or until last follow-up, alongside the Beck Depression and Anxiety Inventories at the same timepoints, and analysed the data with linear and modified Poisson regression. Almost all donors — 98.6%, or 928 of 941 — reported normal-to-high self-esteem before donating, and only 2% to 4% scored in the low range (below 15) during follow-up. Average self-esteem fell by less than one point between pre-donation and follow-up; the authors note these changes reached statistical significance but were not clinically meaningful, all mean changes being under five points. The more useful finding for donor assessment is directional: donors who scored 20 or below before donation gained roughly two points afterwards (p < 0.001), more pre-donation depressive symptoms predicted lower self-esteem at three months (p = 0.006), and increases in self-esteem after donation were accompanied by concurrent reductions in symptoms of both depression and anxiety (p < 0.001). The authors flag one specific limitation — they did not examine whether early recipient graft failure or recipient death affected donor self-esteem, which is precisely the scenario donor advocates worry about most. For UK living donor programmes, this offers evidence-based reassurance for the psychosocial part of donor counselling, while identifying pre-donation depressive symptoms as the signal worth acting on at assessment, with the caveat that a self-selected Canadian and Australian cohort recruited over a decade ago may not fully mirror a contemporary UK donor population.
